title: Kafka: terminology
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: Brokers, clusters, partitions, topics, producers and consumers, and the small difference between using Kafka as a queue or as a stream.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

options.text: An individual server, physical or virtual, that stores data and serves clients.
options.why: Right: a cluster is many brokers.

options.text: A client library that publishes messages.
options.why: That is a producer; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: A single message in a partition as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Messages live in partitions on brokers.

options.text: A configuration file for topics in the majority of deployments.
options.why: It is a server, not a file.

questions.explanation: More brokers mean more data stored and more clients served.

options.text: An ordered, immutable sequence of messages that keeps being appended to, like a log file.
options.why: Right: append-only and ordered.

options.text: A table of rows that can be updated in place without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Messages are never edited.

options.text: A group of consumers that share work.
options.why: That is a consumer group.

options.text: A logical name that producers publish to for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That is a topic; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Partitions are how Kafka scales, since they can be consumed in parallel.

questions.prompt: How do a topic and a partition differ?

options.text: A topic is a logical grouping made of partitions; a partition is a physical grouping that can live on its own broker.
options.why: Right: logical versus physical.

options.text: A topic is physical and a partition is logical as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: They are the same thing under two names in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They differ; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: A topic has exactly one partition.
options.why: A topic can have many.

questions.explanation: Topics are multi-producer: zero, one or many producers can write to a topic.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for creating and processing the messages?

options.text: You, the developer; Kafka is data agnostic and only stores and serves bytes.
options.why: Right: Kafka is the pipe.

options.text: Kafka parses each message and applies your business logic in the majority of deployments.
options.why: It does not look inside values.

options.text: The broker transforms the data to a standard format.
options.why: It does not; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The topic validates every message against a schema automatically as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Not by default; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: That is why producers and consumers carry the business logic.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about using Kafka as a stream rather than a message queue.

options.text: Many independent consumer groups can read the same data.
options.why: Yes: each group has its own offsets.

options.text: The log is retained and can be replayed from any point.
options.why: Yes: reading does not delete it.

options.text: Data is processed continuously as it arrives.
options.why: Yes: real-time flow; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It requires a completely different product from the queue use.
options.why: No: it is the same Kafka log.

questions.explanation: The only difference is how you consume; both modes track progress with offset commits.

questions.prompt: True or false: when Kafka is used as a message queue, a message is deleted as soon as a consumer reads it.

options.text: True
options.why: It does not delete on read.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: retention controls removal.

questions.explanation: Kafka keeps the messages until the retention policy removes them; the consumer just advances its offset.

questions.prompt: In an interview, how do you decide whether to call Kafka a queue or a stream?

options.text: One worker per job suggests a queue; many readers or replay suggests a stream.
options.why: Right: say which one you mean.

options.text: Always call it a stream; queues are a different product without any extra configuration.
options.why: Both uses are valid; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Always call it a queue because streams are slower in a typical production setup.
options.why: Neither is slower inherently.

options.text: It depends on the cloud provider.
options.why: It depends on the use.

questions.explanation: The distinction is small: it is only how you consume.
